title: Sudden wheeze and chest tightness in a 35-year-old man with asthma
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of Jeff, a 35-year-old accountant with lifelong asthma. He comes to the ED with breathlessness, chest tightness and wheeze that started an hour ago after exposure to cat fur and pollen. He cannot finish sentences and is using his accessory muscles. The candidate then interprets his observations, bloods with a venous gas and a chest X-ray, and grades the attack as severe acute asthma. They justify the diagnosis against anaphylaxis, pneumothorax, PE, MI, pneumonia and COPD, outline ED management to the Australian Asthma Handbook, and safety-net with an action plan, a preventer and follow-up.
focus: Acute breathlessness with wheeze: taking a targeted asthma history while treating, screening the dangerous differentials and red flags, grading severity, and managing severe acute asthma in the ED
stem: You are an intern in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital. It is mid-afternoon. Jeff, a 35-year-old accountant, has come in with shortness of breath. He is in an acute bay on a cardiac monitor. A nurse is with you and can carry out your instructions. The nurse has taken his observations, put in an IV cannula and sent bloods with a venous blood gas. The senior ED doctor has requested a portable chest X-ray.
tasks: Take a focused history from Jeff and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. He is very breathless, so keep your questions targeted (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you his observations, blood results with a venous blood gas, and chest X-ray report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Jeff, a 35-year-old accountant. You are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin. You are sitting bolt upright on the trolley, leaning forward with your hands on your knees. You are wheezing loudly enough to be heard and can only say 3 or 4 words before you stop for a breath. You are very distressed and anxious. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they examine.

What the nurse reports at the start (when the candidate asks, or straight away if they do not): "Jeff's friend drove him in about 15 minutes ago. At triage his resp rate was 26, sats 93% on room air, heart rate 112 and regular, BP 134/82, temp 36.8. The repeat a few minutes ago was resp rate 28, sats 92%, heart rate 116, BP 132/80. He had 2 puffs of his own Ventolin through his spacer about an hour ago. The cannula's in, and bloods and a venous gas have gone. The boss has asked for a portable chest X-ray. What would you like me to give him?"

How you change with what the candidate does:

  • If they ask for salbutamol (Ventolin), the nurse asks, "How much, and how?" After the first dose your wheeze is a little quieter and you can say 5 or 6 words at a time. Your hands are a bit shaky.
  • If they ask for oxygen, the nurse asks, "What saturation are you aiming for?" With oxygen your sats come up to about 95%. You are still breathless.
  • If they ask for ipratropium (Atrovent) or prednisolone, the nurse gives it. Nothing changes within the station time.
  • If they call the senior ED doctor, the nurse says: "They're on their way. Keep going."
  • If they ask for a peak flow, the nurse says: "He's too breathless to do a reliable one right now. We can try once he's settled."
  • If they ask you to lie flat, you say, "Can't... lie down... can't breathe."
  • If they ask no one to give you anything for your breathing in the first few minutes, the nurse says: "His sats are 91% now and his resp rate is 30. He's working harder. Do you want to give him something?" You get more distressed.
  • If they ask for the X-ray or the blood results now, the examiner says these will be given in Part 2.

Opening line: "Can't... breathe... it's my asthma..."

History (give only when asked; answer in short bursts of words):

The breathlessness

  • Onset: sudden, about 1 hour ago, while you were at a friend's place. Your friend has a cat, and it is a windy spring day with lots of pollen around.
  • Course: it has got steadily worse since then.
  • Character: "My chest's... really tight." It is tightness, not pain.
  • Wheeze: you can hear yourself wheezing when you breathe out.
  • Severity: you cannot finish a sentence. You have to stop for breath every few words.
  • What helped: you took 2 puffs of Ventolin through your spacer at your friend's place. It helped a little, then got worse again.
  • Previous episodes: yes. You have had similar attacks before, set off by pollen and cat fur.
  • Other triggers (only if asked): colds sometimes set it off; exercise and cold air make you a bit wheezy; no smoke exposure at home or work.
  • Recent control (only if asked): over the last month you have needed Ventolin most days, and you have woken coughing at night a couple of times a week.

Other symptoms (only if asked; all of these are no)

  • No chest pain. No sharp pain when you breathe in. No injury to your chest.
  • No pain that spreads to your arm, neck or jaw. No sweating, no nausea, no palpitations.
  • No swelling of your ankles. You do not get breathless lying flat and you do not wake up gasping for air.
  • No cough before today, no phlegm, no coughing up blood.
  • No fever or shivers. No recent cold or flu. No sick contacts.
  • No pain or swelling in either leg. No recent operations, long flights or time laid up in bed. No previous clots. No cancer. No clotting problems in you or your family.
  • No blue lips that anyone has noticed. You did not choke on anything or breathe anything in.
  • No rash, hives or itch. No swelling of your lips, tongue or face. No tight throat, no change in your voice, no trouble swallowing. No vomiting or tummy cramps. No dizziness or feeling faint.
  • No weight loss, no night sweats, no unusual tiredness.
  • You are not especially tall or thin. No connective tissue problems such as Marfan syndrome.

Past medical history

  • Asthma since you were 8.
  • One previous hospital admission for an asthma attack. You have never been in intensive care and have never needed a breathing tube.
  • No other medical problems.

Medications

  • Ventolin (salbutamol) puffer through a spacer when you need it.
  • You had a few days of steroid tablets during that admission, years ago; none since.
  • You are not on a preventer. Only if asked: a GP gave you a preventer puffer a few years ago, but you stopped it after a few weeks because you felt fine.
  • No other medicines. No problems with aspirin or anti-inflammatories that you know of.

Allergies: hayfever; cat and dog fur; dust. No allergies to any medicines (only if asked).

Family history: both your parents have asthma. You have no brothers or sisters and no children.

Social history

  • You work as an accountant.
  • You have never smoked.
  • Alcohol: about 10 standard drinks a week, socially.
  • No recreational drugs.
  • No pets at home (only if asked).
  • You do not have a written asthma action plan (only if asked).

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you are sure this is an asthma attack. You are very frightened. You are worried that it is your own fault for not taking your asthma medicines properly. You want something to help you breathe.

If the candidate asks whether anything else is worrying you, say: "Is it... my fault?... I stopped... the other puffer."

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: sitting upright and leaning forward, anxious. Using his neck muscles to breathe, with a tracheal tug. Speaks 3 or 4 words per breath. Audible expiratory wheeze from the end of the bed. Alert, not drowsy, not exhausted. Not cyanosed. Weight about 78 kg.
  • Vital signs: as the nurse reported.
  • Skin: no urticaria or flushing.
  • Lips, tongue and face: no angioedema.
  • Upper airway: no stridor; voice normal apart from breathlessness.
  • Hands: warm, capillary refill 2 seconds. No clubbing. Fine tremor (after his Ventolin).
  • Pulse: 116/min, regular, good volume.
  • Blood pressure: 132/80.
  • Face and neck: no central cyanosis. Nasal mucosa pale and swollen. JVP not raised.
  • Trachea: central, with a tracheal tug.
  • Chest inspection: hyperexpanded chest. No scars, wounds or deformity.
  • Palpation: expansion reduced but equal on both sides. No surgical emphysema.
  • Percussion: resonant throughout, equal on both sides.
  • Auscultation: widespread polyphonic expiratory wheeze over both lungs with a prolonged expiratory phase. Air entry reduced but present and equal on both sides; the chest is not silent. No crackles, no bronchial breathing, no pleural rub.
  • Heart: dual heart sounds, no murmurs.
  • Legs: no ankle oedema. Calves soft and non-tender.
  • Peak flow: not done yet; he is too breathless to perform it reliably.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Jeff's identity and asks whether he is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.

Recognises severe respiratory distress and acts before finishing the history: keeps him sitting upright, asks the nurse to give inhaled salbutamol now, asks for oxygen with a stated target (92 to 96%) if SpO2 is below 92%, and calls the senior ED doctor. Then keeps questions short and closed.
check.d: Credit when a bronchodilator is requested and senior help is called within the first few minutes. Accept 92 to 96% (TSANZ/Asthma Handbook) or 93 to 95%.

check.x: History
Characterises the breathlessness:
check.d: Credit when onset and at least 2 of the other 3 are elicited.

kids.x: Onset and course: sudden, 1 hour ago, getting steadily worse
Character: chest tightness, no chest pain
Audible expiratory wheeze; cannot finish sentences
Today's trigger (friend's cat, windy pollen day) and only slight relief from 2 puffs of Ventolin via spacer

check.x: Asks about previous episodes and triggers: similar attacks before with pollen and cat fur; asks about other triggers such as a cold, exercise, cold air, smoke and aspirin or NSAIDs.
Takes the asthma history, including risk factors for a severe attack:
check.d: Credit when the admission and ICU or intubation history are both asked about.

kids.x: Asthma since age 8
One previous admission (one prednisolone course); never in ICU or intubated
Recent control: reliever needed most days and night waking twice a week over the last month

check.x: Takes the medication history: Ventolin via spacer only, not on a preventer (stopped one a few years ago), and no written asthma action plan. Asks about medicine allergies (none).
check.d: Credit when preventer status (none; stopped one) and the absence of a written action plan are both established.

check.x: Screens for the differentials:
check.d: Credit when anaphylaxis, pneumothorax and PE are each screened with at least one relevant question, plus at least one other differential (pneumonia, cardiac or COPD).

kids.x: Pneumothorax: sudden sharp or pleuritic chest pain, chest trauma, connective tissue disorder, smoking
PE: pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, calf pain or swelling, recent surgery or flights, previous clots, malignancy, clotting disorders
Pneumonia: fever, productive cough, recent infection, sick contacts
Cardiac: central or radiating chest pain, sweating, nausea (MI); orthopnoea, PND and ankle swelling (heart failure)
COPD: smoking history (never smoked)
Anaphylaxis: rash or hives, lip or tongue swelling, throat tightness or voice change, vomiting, faintness (all absent)

check.x: Asks about red flags beyond the differentials: blue lips (cyanosis), choking or an inhaled foreign body, and constitutional symptoms such as weight loss and night sweats (malignancy, TB). All absent.
check.d: Credit when at least 2 are asked about.

check.x: Asks about atopy: hayfever, cat and dog fur, dust.
Takes a family history: both parents have asthma; no siblings or children.
Takes a social history: never smoked, about 10 standard drinks a week, no recreational drugs, works as an accountant.
check.d: Credit when at least 3 of the 4 are covered, including smoking.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: believes it is an asthma attack, is very anxious, worries that stopping his medicines caused it, and wants help to breathe.
Examination

General inspection for severity: words per breath, accessory muscle use and tracheal tug, posture, cyanosis, conscious level or exhaustion, and audible wheeze. Uses the nurse's observations (RR 28, SpO2 92% on room air, HR 116).
check.d: Credit when words per breath, accessory muscle use or tracheal tug, and conscious level or exhaustion are assessed, and the nurse's observations are used.

check.x: Respiratory examination:
check.d: Credit when percussion and auscultation are compared side to side and air entry is commented on.

kids.x: Trachea central
Hyperexpanded chest with reduced but equal expansion
Resonant percussion, equal on both sides (against pneumothorax)
Widespread expiratory wheeze with prolonged expiration; air entry present and equal, not a silent chest; no crackles

check.x: Completes the cardiovascular and leg examination: pulse rate and rhythm, heart sounds, JVP, ankle oedema, and soft non-tender calves.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: RR and SpO2 in the yellow zone and worsening between sets; HR white but tachycardic; BP and temperature normal. Calls for senior review now, and a rapid response if any value reaches the red zone.
Interprets the venous gas and bloods:
check.d: Credit for the critical part requires the pCO2 to be interpreted correctly, including what a normal or rising value would mean.

kids.x: Venous gas: low pCO2 with a mild alkalaemia (respiratory alkalosis), appropriate from hyperventilation; states that a normal or rising pCO2 would mean he is tiring (life-threatening)
Bloods: raised eosinophils fitting allergic asthma; normal WCC and CRP against pneumonia; normal potassium as a baseline before repeated salbutamol

check.x: Reads the chest X-ray:

kids.x: Hyperinflated lungs with flattened hemidiaphragms
No pneumothorax and no pneumomediastinum
No consolidation or effusion; heart normal

check.x: Grades the attack as severe acute asthma (unable to finish sentences, accessory muscle use, SpO2 92 to 93%). States there are no life-threatening features: alert, not exhausted, no cyanosis, not a silent chest, SpO2 above 90% and pCO2 not raised.

Gives the diagnosis as a severe acute exacerbation of asthma triggered by cat fur and pollen, on a background of poorly controlled asthma with no preventer. Justifies it with the wheeze and chest tightness, known triggers, previous similar attacks, partial response to Ventolin, family history and atopy.
check.d: Credit when at least 4 supporting features are given.

check.x: Names at least 4 differentials, each with a feature against it from Jeff: anaphylaxis, pneumothorax, PE, MI, pneumonia or COPD.
Management
Escalates and supports: senior ED doctor at the bedside, continuous SpO2 and cardiac monitoring, keeps him sitting upright, and reassesses frequently.
Gives oxygen if SpO2 falls below 92% (he is at 92 to 93% on room air, so watch closely and start oxygen if he drops below 92%), titrated to a target of 92 to 96%; uses oxygen to drive any nebuliser.
Gives salbutamol 12 puffs (100 microgram each) via pMDI and spacer every 20 minutes for the first hour, or 5 mg nebulised (oxygen-driven) if he cannot use the spacer.
Adds ipratropium 8 puffs (21 microgram each) via spacer, or 500 microgram nebulised, every 20 minutes for the first hour.
Gives a systemic corticosteroid within the first hour: prednisolone 37.5 to 50 mg orally (hydrocortisone 100 mg IV 6-hourly if he cannot swallow), continued for 5 to 10 days.

Plans the reassessment after the first hour. For a poor response: IV magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes and a repeat gas. For life-threatening features (drowsiness, exhaustion, cyanosis, silent chest, rising pCO2): ICU review now.

Plans disposition: admits him if he still needs frequent bronchodilator or oxygen, and discharges only once he is stable on room air with his symptoms settled, and a peak flow or FEV1 repeated after treatment shows an adequate response, and he has been observed after his last bronchodilator dose.

Explains in plain words that the airways have tightened and swollen in reaction to the cat and pollen, and answers his worry without blame: stopping the preventer made an attack more likely, and starting one now will protect him. Checks understanding.
Safety netting

Tells Jeff in plain words: call 000 and start asthma first aid if he cannot speak in sentences, his lips turn blue, his reliever gives little or no relief, or he becomes drowsy or exhausted. See a doctor straight away or come back to ED if he needs his reliever again within 3 hours or gets new chest pain.
check.d: Credit when asthma first aid and calling 000 are given with at least 3 specific red flags.

check.x: Arranges the discharge plan: a written asthma action plan, an inhaled corticosteroid-containing preventer (never reliever alone), the prednisolone course, a check of his spacer technique, and allergen avoidance with hayfever treatment.
check.d: Credit when the action plan and the preventer are both included.

check.x: Arranges follow-up: GP review within a week and spirometry once he is well.

part2.lead: Here are his observations, his blood results with the venous gas, and the chest X-ray report.
part2.patient:
Ask this only after the examiner reads question 4, still a little breathless:

  • "So it was my fault for stopping the preventer?"

You are relieved to be breathing more easily. If the candidate explains kindly and without blame, you agree to start the preventer and take the action plan. If they lecture you, go quiet and say, "I just didn't think it mattered." If they use jargon, ask what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Both sets taken on room air in the ED, before any ED treatment. He took 2 puffs of his own reliever at about 13:30.
handover.model:
• Read: at triage, RR 26 and SpO2 93% on room air are in the yellow zone. HR 112, BP 134/82 and temperature 36.8 °C are white. At 14:32, RR 28 and SpO2 92% are still yellow and slightly worse, HR has risen to 116 (white) and BP is 132/80.
  • Meaning: tachypnoea, mild hypoxaemia and tachycardia, worsening, while he is afebrile and normotensive. With his inability to finish sentences, this fits severe acute asthma. A white-zone heart rate does not make him safe.
  • Changes: the yellow zone calls for a clinical review. Here that means senior review now, with treatment started at once and repeat observations. Any red-zone value (RR 30 or more, SpO2 90% or less, HR 140 or more, a change in conscious state) calls for a rapid response.

rows.note: Triage: to acute bay, monitor on; own reliever 2 puffs at about 13:30
Repeat set before medical review; cannula in, bloods and VBG sent

handover.label: Bloods and venous blood gas
handover.result: Venous sample collected at cannulation, 14:28, on room air, before any ED treatment.
handover.model:
• Read: venous pH 7.46 (mildly alkalaemic) with pCO2 33 mmHg (low), normal bicarbonate and base excess, lactate 1.4 and glucose 6.0. Eosinophils raised at 0.8. WCC, neutrophils, Hb and platelets normal; CRP 3. Sodium, potassium (3.9), urea and creatinine normal.
  • Meaning: an acute respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation, which is expected early in an asthma attack. A normal or rising pCO2 in a breathless asthmatic would mean he is tiring, which is a life-threatening feature. A low venous pCO2 makes arterial hypercapnia unlikely. The raised eosinophils fit type 2 (allergic) airway inflammation. A normal WCC and CRP argue against pneumonia.
  • Changes: no arterial gas is needed now. Repeat the gas if he does not respond or tires. Recheck potassium and lactate during repeated salbutamol, because both can be affected by it.

handover.label: Portable chest X-ray
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, portable AP erect (sitting), 14:55 today. Jeff, 35.

Clinical details: 35-year-old man with known asthma. Sudden breathlessness, chest tightness and wheeze for 1 hour after allergen exposure. Unable to complete sentences. SpO2 92% on room air. ?pneumothorax ?consolidation.

Findings:

  • Technical: AP erect film, not rotated, adequate penetration.
  • Lungs: both lungs are hyperinflated, with the right hemidiaphragm below the anterior end of the 7th rib. Mild bilateral peribronchial wall thickening. No consolidation, collapse or mass.
  • Pleura: no pneumothorax on either side. No pleural effusion.
  • Mediastinum: no pneumomediastinum. Trachea central. Mediastinal contours normal.
  • Heart: normal size and outline.
  • Diaphragm: both hemidiaphragms are flattened. Costophrenic angles clear.
  • Bones and soft tissues: no surgical emphysema. No bony abnormality.

Conclusion: hyperinflated lungs with mild peribronchial thickening, in keeping with airway disease. No pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum or consolidation.
handover.model:
• Read: AP erect, adequate film. Hyperinflation with flattened hemidiaphragms and mild peribronchial thickening. No pneumothorax on either side, no pneumomediastinum or surgical emphysema, no consolidation or effusion, and a normal heart.
  • Meaning: this fits acute asthma with air trapping. It excludes pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum (complications of severe asthma that would change management), pneumonia as the trigger, and heart failure. A chest X-ray is not routine in acute asthma; it is done when a complication or another diagnosis is suspected, or there is a poor response.
  • Changes: continue asthma treatment. No antibiotics and no chest drain are needed.

ask: You are now calling the medical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Jeff, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Jeff now, here in the emergency department.
Jeff has settled and is ready to go home. What would you tell him, and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, ED intern; Jeff, 35, accountant.
  • Situation: severe acute asthma. RR 28 and SpO2 92% on room air (yellow zone, worsening), HR 116; cannot finish sentences.
  • Background: sudden tightness and wheeze 1 hour after exposure to cat and pollen; only slight relief from 2 puffs of Ventolin. Asthma since 8, one previous admission (one prednisolone course), never ICU or intubation. No preventer, no action plan. Atopic; never smoked; no medicine allergies.
  • Assessment: accessory muscles; widespread wheeze with air entry; no life-threatening features (alert, not exhausted, no cyanosis, air entry present, SpO2 above 90%, pCO2 low). VBG pH 7.46, pCO2 33: respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation, appropriately low; a normal or rising pCO2 would mean he is tiring (life-threatening). K 3.9: baseline before repeated salbutamol. Eosinophils raised; WCC and CRP normal. CXR hyperinflation, no pneumothorax or consolidation.
  • Recommendation: salbutamol, ipratropium and prednisolone started; oxygen if SpO2 below 92%, target 92 to 96%; please review now and again after the first hour.

Severe acute asthma, triggered by cat fur and pollen, on poorly controlled asthma with no preventer: known allergen trigger, previous identical attacks, partial response to Ventolin, widespread polyphonic wheeze, atopy with raised eosinophils.

Any 4 of the following, each with a feature against it from Jeff, earn item 25.

  • Anaphylaxis: for: sudden wheeze within an hour of allergen exposure; against: no rash, angioedema, stridor or hypotension. If in doubt, IM adrenaline.
  • Pneumothorax: against: no pleuritic pain; percussion and breath sounds equal; none on X-ray.
  • PE: against: no pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, leg swelling or risk factors; widespread wheeze.
  • MI: against: 35, never smoked; tightness without pain, radiation or sweating; clear allergen trigger.
  • Pneumonia: against: afebrile, no productive cough, normal WCC and CRP, no consolidation.
  • COPD: against: never smoked, 35, episodic asthma since childhood.

1. Senior ED doctor at the bedside; continuous monitoring; sit upright. 12-lead ECG (sinus tachycardia expected).
  2. Oxygen if SpO2 falls below 92% (he is at 92 to 93% on room air, so watch closely and start oxygen if he drops below 92%), titrated to SpO2 92 to 96%; oxygen to drive any nebuliser.
  3. Salbutamol 12 puffs via pMDI and spacer every 20 minutes for the first hour (5 mg nebulised, oxygen-driven, if he cannot use the spacer).
  4. Ipratropium 8 puffs (21 microgram) via spacer, or 500 microgram nebulised, every 20 minutes for the first hour.
  5. Prednisolone 37.5 to 50 mg orally within the first hour (hydrocortisone 100 mg IV 6-hourly if he cannot swallow).
  6. Reassess after the first hour. Poor response: IV magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes and a repeat gas. Drowsiness, exhaustion, cyanosis, silent chest or rising pCO2: ICU now.
  7. Admit if he still needs frequent bronchodilator or oxygen; discharge only when stable on room air with an adequate repeat peak flow or FEV1. No antibiotics and no sedation.

• Plain words: the airways tightened and swelled in reaction to the cat and pollen. Without a preventer the airways stay inflamed, so attacks are more likely; it is not about blame.
  • Treatment: written asthma action plan; start an inhaled corticosteroid-containing preventer; finish the prednisolone (5 to 10 days); check his spacer technique.
  • Triggers: avoid cats and dust where possible; treat his hayfever.
  • Red flags: call 000 and start asthma first aid if he cannot speak in sentences, his lips turn blue, his reliever gives little or no relief, or he becomes drowsy or exhausted. See a doctor straight away or come back to ED if he needs his reliever again within 3 hours or gets new chest pain.
  • Follow-up: GP within a week; spirometry once well.

ddx.dx: Severe acute exacerbation of asthma triggered by allergen exposure (cat fur and pollen), on a background of poorly controlled asthma
ddx.for: Sudden chest tightness and audible wheeze after a cat and pollen exposure. He has had previous similar attacks, got partial relief from Ventolin, has had asthma since 8, both parents have asthma and he is atopic. He has widespread wheeze, raised eosinophils and hyperinflation on X-ray.
Sudden wheeze within an hour of allergen exposure.
ddx.against: No urticaria, angioedema, stridor, GI symptoms or hypotension; BP 132/80; isolated lower-airway picture typical of his previous attacks.

ddx.for: Sudden-onset breathlessness in a man with asthma.
ddx.against: No pleuritic chest pain, percussion and breath sounds are equal on both sides, and the X-ray shows no pneumothorax.

ddx.for: Sudden breathlessness with tachycardia and mild hypoxaemia.
ddx.against: No pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, leg swelling, surgery, flights or previous clots, and the widespread wheeze is explained by asthma.

ddx.for: Sudden chest tightness with breathlessness and tachycardia.
ddx.against: He is 35 and has never smoked, has tightness without pain, radiation, sweating or nausea, and has a clear allergen trigger with wheeze.

ddx.for: Acute breathlessness with tachypnoea and hypoxaemia.
ddx.against: He is afebrile with no productive cough or sick contacts, his WCC and CRP are normal and there is no consolidation.

guide:
In Part 1, the nurse gives the opening observations, and Jeff answers in bursts of 3 or 4 words. A good candidate asks for salbutamol and calls for senior help before finishing the history (item 3). Without treatment in the first few minutes, the nurse prompts with a falling SpO2. Give examination findings only when the candidate says what they examine. If the candidate asks for a peak flow, the nurse says he is too breathless. Credit a candidate who does not delay treatment to get one. If results are asked for in Part 1, say they will be given in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over all three results, then ask the four questions in order. Jeff asks his question after question 4 is read.

The source case's red flags for dyspnoea are marked in the history (items 9 and 10: pleuritic pain, features of anaphylaxis, cyanosis, choking or foreign body, constitutional symptoms) and in the severity grading (item 23: inability to speak, cyanosis). Its call for at least 4 differentials is marked in item 25.

A high-performing candidate treats first, then takes a short targeted history. It covers the trigger, previous attacks, admissions and ICU or intubation, the missing preventer and action plan, and a screen for anaphylaxis, pneumothorax, PE, pneumonia, cardiac causes and COPD. They grade severity at the bedside and compare both sides of the chest. In Part 2 they read the low pCO2 as appropriate, know that a normal or rising pCO2 means he is tiring, and confirm there is no pneumothorax. They give the Asthma Handbook doses and plan the reassessment after the first hour. They address Jeff's guilt without blame and send him home with a preventer, an action plan and a GP review.

A borderline candidate takes a long history before giving any bronchodilator. They miss the ICU or intubation question or the missing preventer, do not consider anaphylaxis after an allergen exposure, and do not grade severity. They may call the venous gas "normal", give oxygen without a target, or forget the steroid. Delaying bronchodilator treatment, or sending him home on a reliever alone without an action plan or follow-up, is a serious safety concern.
explain:
Diagnosis: severe acute asthma triggered by allergens

Jeff has a severe acute exacerbation of asthma. It was set off by cat fur and pollen on a background of poorly controlled asthma: he had no preventer, was using his reliever most days and woke at night. Asthma involves bronchoconstriction, airway oedema and inflammation, airway hyperreactivity and, over time, remodelling. The inflammation is typically type 2 (Th2), driven by eosinophils and mast cells, with smooth muscle hypertrophy, mucus plugging and often a blood eosinophilia. Without an inhaled corticosteroid the inflammation goes untreated, so allergen exposure produces a severe attack. The features that support asthma here are wheeze and chest tightness, known triggers, previous similar attacks, a partial response to Ventolin, a family history of asthma and atopy (hayfever, animal fur, dust).

Triggers to ask about: allergens (pollen, animal dander, dust mite, moulds), viral infections (especially rhinovirus), cold dry air, exercise, inhaled irritants (smoke, pollution, perfumes, cleaning products), emotion, aspirin and NSAIDs, and GORD.

The history while treating

  • The attack: onset, trigger, course, reliever use and response.
  • Risk of a fatal attack: previous ICU admission or intubation, hospital admissions and ED visits, oral steroid courses, high reliever use, no preventer, and no written action plan.
  • The differentials: pneumothorax (sudden pleuritic pain, trauma, tall and thin, connective tissue disorder, emphysema, smoking); PE (pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, calf swelling, surgery, flights, previous clots, thrombophilia, malignancy); pneumonia (fever, productive cough); heart failure (orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling); MI (central or radiating pain, sweating, nausea); COPD (smoking). Allergen exposure with wheeze should also prompt a quick check for anaphylaxis (rash, lip or tongue swelling, throat tightness or voice change, vomiting, faintness or hypotension), because anaphylaxis changes first-line treatment to IM adrenaline. If there is any doubt about anaphylaxis, give adrenaline 0.5 mg IM (1 mg/mL) into the anterolateral thigh (ASCIA adult dose; 0.01 mg/kg, maximum 0.5 mg) and repeat every 5 minutes as needed; it will not harm a severe asthma attack. Jeff has none of these features: his picture is isolated lower-airway obstruction, like his previous attacks.

Red flags in any breathless patient

  • Breathlessness with wheeze or stridor and inability to speak: airway threat from an inhaled foreign body, anaphylaxis or severe asthma.
  • Pleuritic chest pain: PE, pneumothorax or pneumonia.
  • Central cyanosis: failing gas exchange.
  • Constitutional symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fevers): malignancy or TB.

Grading severity (Australian Asthma Handbook, adults)

  • Mild to moderate: can walk and speak whole sentences in one breath; SpO2 above 94%.
  • Severe (any of): accessory muscle use or tracheal tug; unable to complete sentences in one breath; obvious respiratory distress; SpO2 90 to 94%.
  • Life-threatening (any of): reduced consciousness or collapse; exhaustion; cyanosis; SpO2 below 90%; PaO2 below 60 mmHg; PaCO2 above 45 mmHg; poor respiratory effort or a silent chest; arrhythmia.

Jeff is severe: he cannot finish sentences, uses his neck muscles and has a tracheal tug, with SpO2 92 to 93%. He has no life-threatening features. Do not delay treatment to measure peak flow in a severe attack.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: RR and SpO2 in the yellow zone and worsening call for a clinical review, here a senior review now. Any red-zone value calls for a rapid response.
  • Venous gas: early in an attack, hyperventilation drives the pCO2 down (respiratory alkalosis). A "normal" or rising pCO2 in a breathless asthmatic is a warning that he is tiring. A low venous pCO2 makes arterial hypercapnia unlikely. Repeated salbutamol can lower potassium and raise lactate, so recheck them.
  • Bloods: raised eosinophils fit type 2 inflammation. A normal WCC and CRP argue against pneumonia.
  • Chest X-ray: not routine in acute asthma. It is done when a pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum or consolidation is suspected, or when the response is poor. Here it shows hyperinflation only.

Management in the ED (Australian Asthma Handbook; eTG)

  1. Escalate and monitor: senior doctor, continuous monitoring, sit upright.
  2. Oxygen if SpO2 is below 92% (he is at 92 to 93% on room air, so watch closely and start oxygen if he drops below 92%), titrated to a target of 92 to 96%. Do not give oxygen routinely when SpO2 is 92% or above, and avoid pushing it above 96%. Use oxygen to drive any nebuliser.
  3. Salbutamol: 12 puffs (100 microgram each) via pMDI and spacer every 20 minutes for the first hour. If he cannot use a spacer, give 5 mg nebulised, driven by oxygen. Life-threatening asthma needs continuous nebulised salbutamol.
  4. Ipratropium in severe or life-threatening asthma: 8 puffs (21 microgram each) via spacer, or 500 microgram nebulised, every 20 minutes for the first hour.
  5. Systemic corticosteroid within the first hour: prednisolone 37.5 to 50 mg orally, then daily for 5 to 10 days. Use hydrocortisone 100 mg IV 6-hourly if he cannot take tablets.
  6. Reassess after the first hour. If the response is poor, give IV magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes and repeat the gas. Life-threatening features or a rising pCO2 need ICU review for possible intubation. Do not sedate him, and give antibiotics only if there is evidence of bacterial infection.
  7. Disposition: admit if he still needs frequent bronchodilator or oxygen. Discharge only once he is stable on room air and his symptoms have settled, and a peak flow or FEV1 repeated after treatment shows an adequate response, and he has been observed after his last bronchodilator dose.

Discharge, safety netting and follow-up

Before Jeff goes home he needs a written asthma action plan and an inhaled corticosteroid-containing preventer: preferably budesonide-formoterol as maintenance-and-reliever therapy (or a regular ICS-LABA at an appropriate dose); a reliever alone, or low-dose ICS alone without review, is not enough after a severe flare-up. He finishes his prednisolone course and has his spacer technique checked. He should avoid his allergens where he can and have his allergic rhinitis treated (an intranasal corticosteroid), because treating it improves asthma control. He should not feel blamed: explain that the preventer treats the inflammation that makes attacks more likely.

Teach him asthma first aid: sit upright; give 4 separate puffs through the spacer, 4 breaths after each; wait 4 minutes; if no improvement, give 4 more puffs; if still no improvement, call 000 and keep giving 4 puffs every 4 minutes until help arrives. Call 000 straight away if he is not breathing, suddenly worse, cannot speak, has blue lips or collapses. More broadly, he should call 000 and start asthma first aid if he cannot speak in sentences, his lips turn blue, his reliever gives little or no relief, or he becomes drowsy or exhausted. He should see a doctor straight away or come back to ED if he needs his reliever again within 3 hours or gets new chest pain. Arrange a GP review within a week and spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility once he is well to confirm the diagnosis. The GP can also arrange a referral to a respiratory physician or allergist; FeNO, blood eosinophils and IgE help characterise type 2 asthma. He should also have annual influenza vaccination.
points: Treat first in a breathless asthmatic who cannot finish sentences: inhaled salbutamol, controlled oxygen and senior help come before the full history.
Ask every person with asthma about previous ICU admission or intubation, admissions, oral steroids, reliever use, whether they take a preventer and whether they have a written action plan.

Grade severity at the bedside (Australian Asthma Handbook): inability to complete sentences or accessory muscle use means severe; drowsiness, exhaustion, cyanosis, a silent chest, SpO2 below 90% or a raised pCO2 means life-threatening.
In acute asthma the pCO2 should be low. A normal or rising pCO2 means the patient is tiring and needs ICU review.

Severe asthma in the ED: salbutamol 12 puffs via spacer and ipratropium 8 puffs every 20 minutes for the first hour, oxygen if SpO2 is below 92% titrated to 92 to 96%, prednisolone 37.5 to 50 mg within the hour, and IV magnesium for a poor response.
Never discharge on a reliever alone: give an inhaled corticosteroid-containing preventer, a written action plan, asthma first aid and 000 advice, and a GP review within a week.
